“He spread no ideas that some office clerk could not equally well have spread for him.
“But precisely because he had no ideas to spread, he caused human slaughter, violated justice, and ruined whole states in order to spread—this idea.”

Today, in 1948, everyone would immediately assume this was about poor Adolf Hitler and would consider it an accurate description of him. But it appeared in a journal edited by Franz Blei in 1913, Der Lose Vogel, published by K. Wolff in Leipzig, p. 246. And it refers to Cecil Rhodes.
Son of this consecration, you should tremble! Listen and suffer! (Th. Däubler, By the Sea).
The water demon dies and Pan no longer smiles (Christmas Triptych).

Some beat from a deeper, hidden rhythm in Gerhard Nebel’s lecture last night in Werdohl has not stopped pounding inside me since then. It began during the lecture at the passage and the word “earth-burrower.”
Now it is flowing into the utterly overwhelming rhythm of Theodor Däubler’s “Ethiopian Dance of Death.”
I am certain that great things will become clear if Gerhard Nebel reads this Dance of Death aloud to us one day.
Happiness: I walked out of the sermon.
My child, without seeing me do it, did exactly the same and went home as well, because it had become far too tasteless for him.
Genius, whom you do not abandon!
Poor Konrad Weiß and his poem of 1933.

Here the desperate Hohenstaufen from Schwäbisch Hall breaks loose; the trampled South German peasant of 1525; the Westphalian Anabaptist broken on the wheel in 1535 lashes out once more; the betrayed citizen of 1813; the humiliated democrat of 1848; the defeated victor of the battles of the First World War; the mercenary cheated of his pay by world history.

The poor, tormented foot soldiers of all those who possess power and all those who claim to possess right—they all break loose and strike out once more in madness before finally recognizing the identity of Christianity and Judaism and sinking away as victims.
We were all still deeply moved by a sentence from Ernst Jünger’s Radiations that Gerhard Nebel quoted the evening before last in Werdohl.
When Jünger’s son Ernst died, Jünger said:
“The good boy! He always wanted to equal his father; now he has done better.”
The simplest, deepest, and most beautiful words a father could speak in such a situation.
How sad that reading many passages from these Radiations will have to be a great disappointment to Gueydan and cause him deep pain.
What confusion in the so-called battle lines!
“Heaven and earth will pass away”—is that not the purest nihilism?
“But my words will not pass away”—is that not the purest existentialism?
Again and again I return to a theory of the Italian jurist Gabba.

Under a occupatio bellica, a military occupation, the population of the occupied territory—as distinct both from its former state and from the occupying power—is a separate third entity. It cannot simply be treated as an object, at least not when it is the civilized population of a civilized country.

Gabba was really right: the population of occupied territory ought to be understood as a legal subject in its own right. For its connection with its previous government—the government of the occupied state—is precarious.
After a debellatio, the complete defeat and destruction of the occupied state as a political power, no such relationship is possible at all.

According to the <classical> doctrine, the population of occupied territory is famously required to serve two masters: the absent old master with loyalty and fidelity, and the new master who is physically present with legal obedience.
The Belgians played such an important role in this classical international-law theory of occupation.
In 1914–18, because of their particular situation, they strongly emphasized attachment to the absent government as a general principle and a general right.

But the entire construction of this double relationship becomes completely meaningless once the state power of the occupied territory has been destroyed or is entirely in the hands of the occupying power. Then there is no longer any possibility of loyalty or fidelity, unless the occupying power is regarded as succeeding to the old government’s right to loyalty—which Hall rejects.

What remains is pure legality: obedience to the measures of the occupation authorities. But then it ought to be self-evident that the population cannot simply disappear into a void in international law if the territory itself is not annexed.
The enemy is not something that is simply expelled or excreted.

The relationship between friend and enemy is not the relationship between food and excrement. It is much closer to mixture and mating: the wedding night of opposites, a Heraclitean orgy. That is true even in civil war, so long as the war between citizens remains a war between brothers.
Civil war is the great war of mixture.
Marxist class struggle is no longer a civil war.
There is something horrifying in this kind of hostility: the banquet of Leviathan and, finally, Köppelsbleek, the flayer’s pit.
The defeated man is thrown onto the dung heap—or, in modern terms, into the rubbish bin. He is handed over to the knacker.

He wanted to force his way into the class that ruled the world and gain access to its secret. He did not want to tear that secret away from them. He merely wanted to share in it. He wanted to be admitted to the exclusive club, finally to become a truly great gentleman, a lord. But that secret really did lie in the idea of race.

Power is not something evil. It is something utterly alien—just as alien to the person who possesses power as it is to the person subjected to it. That is why struggles for power become so intense between relatives, between brothers, between father and son.
I think of Otto the Great’s struggle with his brothers, who had to be killed, or of the wars of extermination between the Red Rose and the White Rose, and similar cases.
Power remains completely “other” even in relation to the individual clothed in power.
Naturally, it remains equally alien to the person subjected to it.
(Here it touches the definition of God: power does, after all, come from God.) And here lies the great problem: all power comes either from God or from the people.
From the people—in the sense of an identity between power and powerlessness, in the sense that the command is made legitimate by obedience.

Do I have the right to speak about power? I think one can say that I do. I have experienced every kind of power on my own body. I have sat in the belly of the fish. I have observed power from close by and from far away. I have always looked for good places from which to observe it, and I have found them: on the left ear or the right ear of Leviathan, inside his jaws, and on his tail. And finally: I myself have never sought power and have never possessed power. Nor am I sitting somewhere safely out of range. It is not in my nature to call upon poor, tormented people to resist while I myself remain in the most comfortable shelter.

And when, twenty years ago, I often used the word “existential,” I used it existentially, not yet existentialistically. It was still closer to Søren Kierkegaard’s room than it is in the hands of those who exploit him today; closer to Barbey and Villiers than to the present-day profiteurs de Léon Bloy, the profiteers of Léon Bloy.
Do we still remember those critical schoolmasters who portrayed Cicero and Seneca to us as cowards, weaklings, opportunists, and mere rhetoricians?
A well-fed professor, comfortably established and wrapped securely in the wool of pre-war prosperity, found Cicero and Seneca insufficiently heroic.
Seneca perhaps received a little mercy. But they tore Cicero apart, with the great Theodor Mommsen leading the charge.
Exul in patria mea—an exile in my own country.
Compared with these Californian radio heroes, one could easily be tempted to start boasting.
I could say in the style of Walt Whitman:
Whoever speaks of law wants to deceive.
Whoever speaks of power wants to reveal.
The powerful man does not speak of power. He does not think about power.

The word is a sign from beyond. It is a phonetic hieroglyph. It is an echo that shares in primordial worlds. This is what Konrad Weiß means by the creatureliness of the word: the word as distinct from the neutralizing thing called language, as Theodor Haecker speaks of it.
That is my hopeless position within a German Catholicism devoted to neutralization, in which the objective has become nothing more than a “bourgeois concept of preservation.”
Theodor Haecker’s polemic against my concept of the political also came out of this neutralism.
How alone I stand there, with poor Konrad Weiß.
Even the weakling Maritain, and his hate-filled Raïssa.
“Now you stand naked, naked as at birth, in desolate spaces.”
What did humanity need when these weapons of annihilation arrived?
Then: ratio, reason—the dictatorship of reason.
Today: a pouvoir spirituel, a spiritual power.
Today: the leap into an absolutism infinitely more absolute. That would be the leap into the realm of freedom—naturally only for those who are free.
The leap into the fantastic and utopian, into Huxley’s Brave New World—or onto the Way of the Cross of God made man.
The answer has already been given.
Everything has already been accomplished, and all that you do is answer.
What humanity needs is a martyr, not a Napoleon.
The martyr is at once a subhuman—from the viewpoint of the ruling type—and a superhuman, seen in truth.
The deficiency that is not a zero point.
Power: the true motive behind the will to power can only be the right to renounce power.
We seek to take possession of the world so that we can throw it away.
Every other motive is meaningless or comic. Or do you really want to take possession of the world so that you can enjoy it?
Well then, cheers, you poor Sybarite. You poor pleasure-seeker.
The world will certainly serve you.
Avoir pour savoir—to have in order to know.
Le maquis est une création posthume.
The Resistance is a posthumous creation.
Les attaques de la presse sont un brevet d’honnêteté pour ses victimes.
